reference.source: Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension / Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology
clinicalPearls: Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant cause of early-onset, low-renin hypertension caused by gain-of-function variants in the beta or gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel (SCNN1B, SCNN1G)
The variants disrupt channel removal from the collecting-duct membrane, so ENaC remains constitutively active regardless of aldosterone
The typical picture is hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, and characteristically both renin and aldosterone are suppressed
It behaves like a mineralocorticoid excess state but there is no excess hormone, hence the older term pseudoaldosteronism
Because the defect is at the sodium channel itself, an ENaC-blocking potassium-sparing diuretic (amiloride or triamterene) is effective, whereas an aldosterone-receptor antagonist is not
Dietary salt restriction complements pharmacological ENaC blockade
Consider it in young patients with resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia and a suppressed renin and aldosterone, especially with a supportive family history
reference.pathophysiology: Liddle syndrome is driven by activating variants in the SCNN1B or SCNN1G genes that encode the beta and gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel in the distal nephron. These variants typically delete or alter a cytoplasmic motif that is normally recognised by the ubiquitin ligase machinery, so the channel is not internalised and degraded and instead accumulates at the apical membrane. The result is excessive, aldosterone-independent sodium reabsorption with parallel renal loss of potassium and hydrogen ion, generating volume expansion, hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The expanded volume and raised pressure suppress renin release and therefore aldosterone secretion, giving the paradoxical combination of a mineralocorticoid-excess phenotype with low aldosterone.
additionalDifferentials: Licorice ingestion or exogenous mineralocorticoid effect
additionalInvestigations: Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed)
Serum potassium and bicarbonate to document hypokalaemic alkalosis
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio to exclude primary hyperaldosteronism
Assessment of therapeutic response to ENaC blockade versus aldosterone antagonism
Screening for licorice and exogenous mineralocorticoids
Molecular genetic testing of SCNN1B and SCNN1G
redFlags: Severe or resistant hypertension in a young person
Profound hypokalaemia with muscle weakness or arrhythmia
End-organ damage from long-standing untreated hypertension
Strong family history of early hypertension or premature stroke
reference.prognosis: With ENaC-blocking therapy and salt restriction, blood pressure and potassium usually normalise and long-term outlook is good; untreated disease carries the cardiovascular and renal risks of chronic hypertension.
pitfalls: Treating with an aldosterone-receptor antagonist, which is ineffective because the defect is downstream of the receptor at the channel
Misdiagnosing it as primary hyperaldosteronism despite the suppressed aldosterone
Overlooking the diagnosis in young hypertensive patients without checking renin and aldosterone
Failing to screen and counsel first-degree relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
management: Treat with ENaC-blocking potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride or triamterene) as the specific and effective therapy
Combine dietary sodium restriction with pharmacological ENaC blockade
Avoid aldosterone-receptor antagonists, which are ineffective because aldosterone is already suppressed
Correct hypokalaemia and monitor blood pressure, serum potassium and acid-base status
Advise avoidance of liquorice and exogenous mineralocorticoids
Manage the cardiovascular and renal risks associated with chronic hypertension
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and screen first-degree relatives
